subject: Computer Systems
title: Operating System Concepts
subtitle: Processes, Memory Virtualization & Storage
author: Abraham Silberschatz, Peter B. Galvin & Greg Gagne

pages.title: Operating System Foundations & Services
bulletPoints: The Operating System as an extended machine (clean abstractions) and resource allocator (CPU, memory, disk).
Dual-mode operation: User Mode vs Kernel Mode protected by hardware privilege rings and mode bits.
System Calls: Controlled software traps transferring execution safely from user mode into OS kernel handlers.
Core OS architecture: Monolithic kernels (Linux), Microkernels (Mach/QNX), Hybrid kernels (Windows/macOS).

pages.title: Processes & Process Control Blocks
bulletPoints: Process definition: A program in execution containing program counter, stack, data section, and heap.
Process states: New, Ready, Running, Waiting (Blocked), and Terminated state transition diagram.
Process Control Block (PCB): Storing process ID, state, CPU registers, scheduling priority, and open file descriptors.
Context Switching: Saving the state of the running process and restoring another process; kernel overhead metrics.

pages.title: Process Creation & Inter-Process Communication
bulletPoints: Process hierarchy: The init/systemd root process; fork() duplicating processes and execve() loading binaries.
Zombie and Orphan processes: Handling terminated children and adoption by init.
IPC models: Shared memory (high speed, requires synchronization) vs Message Passing (pipes, message queues, sockets).
Unix pipes: Anonymous unidirectional byte streams between related processes; named pipes (FIFOs) across filesystem.

pages.title: Threads & Multi-Threading Models
bulletPoints: Thread concept: Lightweight unit of CPU utilization sharing code, data, and OS resources with peer threads.
Thread control block: Private thread ID, program counter, register set, and private execution stack.
User threads vs Kernel threads: Many-to-One, One-to-One (standard Linux pthreads), and Many-to-Many models.
Thread pools: Amortizing thread creation overhead by maintaining worker queues for incoming tasks.

pages.title: CPU Scheduling Concepts & Metrics
bulletPoints: CPU-I/O burst cycle: Processes alternate between intensive CPU computation and waiting for I/O completion.
Preemptive vs Non-preemptive scheduling: Forcibly interrupting running threads vs waiting for voluntary yield.
Scheduling metrics: CPU Utilization, Throughput, Turnaround Time, Waiting Time, and Response Time.
Dispatcher: The module that gives control of the CPU to the process selected by the short-term scheduler.

pages.title: Classic Scheduling Algorithms
bulletPoints: First-Come, First-Served (FCFS): Simple FIFO queue; prone to the Convoy Effect where short jobs wait behind long ones.
Shortest Job First (SJF) & Shortest Remaining Time First (SRTF): Mathematically optimal average wait time, but requires burst prediction.
Round Robin (RR): Preemptive time-slicing using a fixed time quantum q; balancing responsiveness and context switch overhead.
Priority Scheduling: Assigning priorities; preventing starvation of low-priority tasks through aging techniques.

pages.title: Multi-Level Queue & Multi-Core Scheduling
bulletPoints: Multi-Level Feedback Queue (MLFQ): Dynamically adjusting thread priorities based on observed CPU burst behavior.
I/O-bound interactive processes stay at high priority; CPU-intensive batch jobs descend to lower priority levels.
Multiprocessor scheduling: Asymmetric multiprocessing (master/worker) vs Symmetric Multiprocessing (SMP).
Processor affinity (Soft vs Hard affinity) and NUMA-aware scheduling to maximize local cache hits.

pages.title: Process Synchronization & Critical Sections
bulletPoints: Race conditions: Inconsistent system state when multiple concurrent threads read and write shared data without synchronization.
The Critical Section Problem: A section of code accessing shared resources; requires Mutual Exclusion, Progress, and Bounded Waiting.
Peterson's Algorithm: Software solution for two processes using turn variables and flag arrays with memory barrier requirements.
Hardware synchronization primitives: Atomic Test-and-Set and Compare-and-Swap (CAS) CPU instructions.

pages.title: Mutex Locks, Semaphores & Monitors
bulletPoints: Mutex locks: Binary locking primitives with acquire() and release() enforcing mutual exclusion.
Counting Semaphores: Integer variables initialized to N resource slots, accessed via wait() [P] and signal() [V].
Spinlocks vs Sleeping locks: Busy-waiting on multiprocessor systems vs context switching to sleep queues.
Monitors: High-level language synchronization construct encapsulating shared variables and condition variables (wait/signal).

pages.title: Classic Synchronization Problems
bulletPoints: The Bounded-Buffer (Producer-Consumer) problem: Managing full, empty, and mutex semaphores across circular buffers.
The Readers-Writers problem: Permitting concurrent read operations while ensuring exclusive write operations without starvation.
The Dining Philosophers problem: Preventing deadlock and starvation when multiple threads acquire circular resources.
Deadlock-free philosopher solutions: Resource hierarchy ordering and asymmetrical pickup rules.

pages.title: Deadlock Characterization & Prevention
bulletPoints: The four Coffman conditions for deadlock: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait.
Resource Allocation Graphs (RAG): Cycle detection in systems with single resource instances indicates deadlock.
Deadlock Prevention: Eliminating at least one Coffman condition (e.g. strict global resource numbering for circular wait).
Deadlock Avoidance: Operating system checks if resource allocation leaves system in a provably Safe State.

pages.title: Banker's Algorithm for Deadlock Avoidance
bulletPoints: Safe vs Unsafe states: An unsafe state is not a deadlock, but it has the potential to lead to a deadlock.
Banker's Algorithm data structures: Available vector, Max matrix, Allocation matrix, and Need matrix (Need = Max - Allocation).
Safety algorithm: Searching for an execution sequence where all processes can finish with currently available resources.
Resource request algorithm: Granting requests only if the hypothetical resulting state remains provably safe.

pages.title: Deadlock Detection & Recovery
bulletPoints: Deadlock detection in systems with multiple resource instances: Graph reduction algorithms on allocation/request matrices.
Detection frequency trade-offs: Checking on every request vs running background periodic sweeps.
Recovery strategies: Process termination (aborting all deadlocked processes vs aborting one by one until cycle breaks).
Resource preemption: Rolling back victim processes to checkpoints and preventing victim starvation.

pages.title: Main Memory Management & Address Binding
bulletPoints: Address binding stages: Compile time (absolute addresses), Load time (relocatable addresses), Execution time (dynamic MMU translation).
Memory Management Unit (MMU): Hardware device mapping logical addresses to physical RAM addresses.
Relocation and Limit registers: Enforcing memory protection and process address space confinement.
Contiguous memory allocation: Fixed partitions vs Variable partitions; First-fit, Best-fit, and Worst-fit strategies.

pages.title: Fragmentation & Paging Mechanisms
bulletPoints: External fragmentation: Total memory space is sufficient, but storage is fragmented into unusable tiny holes (solved by compaction).
Internal fragmentation: Allocated memory blocks are slightly larger than requested data (e.g. page boundaries).
Paging concept: Breaking physical memory into fixed-size Frames and logical memory into same-sized Pages.
Page table lookups: Page number (p) indexes into page table to retrieve physical frame base address (f).

pages.title: Hardware Page Tables & Translation Lookaside Buffers
bulletPoints: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB): High-speed hardware associative cache storing recent virtual-to-physical translations.
Effective Memory Access Time: EAT = Hit_Ratio × (TLB_access + RAM_access) + (1 - Hit_Ratio) × (TLB_access + 2 × RAM_access).
TLB reach: The amount of memory accessible from the TLB (Number of entries × Page size).
ASIDs: Address-Space Identifiers in TLB entries preventing full TLB flushes on process context switches.

pages.title: Hierarchical & Inverted Page Tables
bulletPoints: The challenge of large 64-bit address spaces: A single flat page table would require terabytes of physical memory.
Multi-level hierarchical page tables: Two-level, three-level, and four-level page tables paged on demand.
Hashed page tables: Using hash tables keyed by virtual page number for 64-bit sparse address spaces.
Inverted page tables: Exactly one entry per physical frame in RAM, indexed by PID and virtual page number.

pages.title: Virtual Memory & Demand Paging
bulletPoints: Virtual memory: Separating user logical memory from physical memory; running programs larger than physical RAM.
Demand Paging: Loading pages into physical memory only when they are accessed during program execution.
Page fault sequence: MMU trap -> OS saves registers -> check internal tables -> allocate free frame -> disk read -> update page table -> restart instruction.
Pure demand paging: Starting execution with zero pages in memory, generating page faults as instructions execute.

pages.title: Page Replacement Algorithms
bulletPoints: Page replacement need: Resolving out-of-memory conditions when a page fault occurs and no free frames exist.
FIFO (First-In, First-Out): Replacing oldest page; subject to Belady's Anomaly (more frames causing more page faults!).
Optimal Algorithm (OPT): Replacing page that will not be used for the longest period of time (theoretical benchmark).
LRU (Least Recently Used): Replacing page unused for the longest time; implemented via counters or stack structures.

pages.title: Second-Chance, Clock & Working-Set Model
bulletPoints: Second-Chance (Clock) algorithm: FIFO replacement enhanced with reference bit; giving active pages a second chance.
Enhanced second-chance: Combining reference bit (r) and dirty bit (m) into four priority classes (r, m).
Thrashing: When a system spends more time servicing page faults and swapping than executing user instructions.
Working-Set Model: Tracking pages referenced in the last Delta time window to allocate sufficient frames and prevent thrashing.

pages.title: Mass Storage & Disk Scheduling
bulletPoints: Hard Disk Drives (HDDs): Platters, read/write heads, tracks, sectors, seek time, rotational latency, transfer rate.
Solid-State Drives (SSDs): Flash memory cells, pages (read/write unit), blocks (erase unit), wear leveling, TRIM command.
Disk scheduling algorithms: FCFS, SSTF (Shortest Seek Time First), SCAN (Elevator algorithm), C-SCAN (Circular SCAN).
RAID redundancy: Mirroring (RAID 1), Block interleaved parity (RAID 5), Dual parity (RAID 6).

pages.title: File System Interface & Directory Structure
bulletPoints: File concept: Contiguous logical address space abstracting persistent secondary storage.
File attributes: Name, identifier, type, location, size, protection permissions, timestamps.
File access methods: Sequential access (tape/stream model) vs Direct / Random access (block seeking).
Directory structures: Single-level, Two-level, Tree-structured directories, and Acyclic-graph directories (hard/soft links).

pages.title: File System Implementation & Inodes
bulletPoints: Disk block allocation: Contiguous allocation, Linked allocation, and Indexed allocation (Inodes).
Unix Inode architecture: Direct block pointers, single indirect pointer, double indirect pointer, triple indirect pointer.
Free-space management: Bit vectors (bitmaps), linked free space lists, and grouping/counting techniques.
VFS (Virtual File System): Kernel abstraction layer providing standard POSIX file operations over ext4, NTFS, NFS.

pages.title: File System Reliability & Journaling
bulletPoints: Consistency checking: fsck scanning disk metadata after unexpected crashes to rebuild allocation bitmaps.
Journaling / Write-Ahead Logging file systems (ext3, ext4, NTFS): Recording metadata updates to journal before committing to disk.
Log recovery: Fast replay of journal transactions upon reboot, reducing recovery time from hours to seconds.
Log-Structured File Systems (LFS): Writing all file data and metadata sequentially in continuous disk segments.

pages.title: OS Security, Virtualization & Hypervisors
bulletPoints: Protection domain: Access matrices specifying rights of domains over objects; Access Control Lists (ACLs) vs Capabilities.
Type-1 (Bare Metal) Hypervisors (Xen, ESXi) vs Type-2 (Hosted) Hypervisors (KVM, VirtualBox).
Hardware-assisted virtualization: Intel VT-x and AMD-V extended page tables (EPT) eliminating binary translation.
Containers vs Virtual Machines: OS-level virtualization sharing common kernel via Linux namespaces and cgroups (Docker).
